overview: The atlas labels this polygon “Maya Yucateco” from 1492 to 1500, but it was not one country, empire, ethnicity, or securely attested shared self-name. Northern Yucatán held towns, houses, alliance networks, and rival lordships; the shape stretches south to Calakmul, Lamanai, and Tikal while excluding Cozumel, Tulum, and Cabo Catoche. That makes it an editorial region, not a surveyed border. Named excavations reveal farming households, tools, foods, water works, movement, and selective continuities, but no site stands for the whole shape. Later Maya-language and Spanish records add family, political, and ritual detail only when their colonial dates and purposes stay visible. Columbus did not reach Yucatán during these eight years. The first recorded encounter conventionally linked to Maya traders came near Honduras in 1502, and documented Yucatán landfalls came later. No surviving northern-Yucatán text is securely dated to exactly 1492 to 1500, so this card will not invent a glyph sample. At 1500 the atlas merely renames much of the area “maya.” Nothing in that software seam records a fall, migration, or population replacement; communities and regional traditions continued beyond the map’s artificial endpoint.

periods.title: 1492 to 1493: an atlas layer covers a plural region
periods.summary: The exact feature first appears in 1492, but that is a cartographic choice rather than a kingdom's founding. Mayapán's former center had already broken apart, and later documents reconstruct multiple lordships and shifting relationships. This one-year teaching slice does not claim a synchronized political change.

periods.title: 1493 to 1494: Caribbean voyages remain elsewhere
periods.summary: Columbus's voyages changed Caribbean worlds, yet no surviving record places a Spanish landing or meeting in northern Yucatán during this slice. Events elsewhere still mattered to later history, but the card resists making 1492 an instant local contact date.

periods.title: 1494 to 1495: households keep regional economies moving
periods.summary: Farming, food preparation, building maintenance, household production, and exchange kept regional economies moving through seasonal cycles. Mayapán evidence mostly predates this slice, and modern food-security research is only comparative, so no single household schedule can be assigned to every town in this polygon.

periods.title: 1495 to 1496: water shapes local choices
periods.summary: Porous limestone, seasonal rain, cenotes, wells, and cisterns created different water strategies across the peninsula. Natural openings supplied some communities, while built storage mattered elsewhere. The map color hides these sharp environmental and engineering differences.

periods.title: 1496 to 1497: markets and routes connect distinct communities
periods.summary: Obsidian, ceramics, salt, cotton, honey, wax, marine foods, ornaments, and metal objects moved through overlapping networks. Similar goods do not prove political unity. Traders, carriers, canoe crews, producers, brokers, and consumers could connect places while maintaining different loyalties and languages.

periods.title: 1497 to 1498: books and specialists preserve knowledge
periods.summary: Late Postclassic Maya scribes and ritual specialists used hieroglyphic books and sophisticated calendrical knowledge. Surviving screenfold manuscripts have broad or uncertain dates and provenances, however, so none can honestly be stamped “written here in 1497.”

periods.title: 1498 to 1499: later records reveal power with caution
periods.summary: Later colonial records show tribute cloth and labor demands, while conquest histories reveal negotiation, coercion, rivalry, and resistance after 1517. Neither source is an exact 1498 diary. No surviving Spanish account records direct northern-Yucatán contact in this year, so later power evidence and documentary silence stay separate.

periods.title: 1499 to 1500: the id ends, communities continue
periods.summary: At 1500 the exact id disappears and many interior probes return to the broad atlas label “maya.” The file records no conquest, epidemic, abandonment, or coordinated political change. It is an editorial seam, years before securely documented Spanish contact in Yucatán.

sections.title: Read an atlas label without inventing one Maya country

items.text: “Maya Yucateco” is a modern atlas label. Yucatec Maya is a useful present-day language name, but people around 1492 belonged to particular towns, households, lineages, patrons, and lordships. The evidence does not reveal one state, national border, or universal self-name matching this polygon.

The exact polygon appears only in the 1492 file. It contains sampled Mérida, Mayapán, Chichén Itzá, Maní, Campeche, Calakmul, Lamanai, and Tikal, yet excludes sampled Cozumel, Tulum, Chetumal, Cabo Catoche, and Isla Mujeres. Geometry this inconsistent cannot serve as an ethnic survey.

The same encoded boundary shares one arc with an atlas feature called “garifuna.” Garifuna history belongs to a much later Caribbean colonial setting, so this is an obvious topology error, not a 1492 frontier. Fun fact: sometimes a map accidentally introduces neighbors who have not arrived yet.

At 1400 many inland probes are simply “maya”; at 1492 they become “maya-yucateco”; at 1500 they become “maya” again. Those renamings happen inside the database. No source records entire communities changing identity together at midnight when the map switches files.

Modern speakers use names such as maaya and maaya t’aan, but a living autonym cannot be pasted backward as proof that everyone used it identically in 1492. This card uses “Yucatec Maya” descriptively while keeping local identities and modern Maya peoples visible.

sections.title: Meet towns, lordships, alliances, rivals, and a distant Atlantic

items.text: Mayapán was a major walled center before the target interval, but radiocarbon work and historical reconstructions place its political collapse in the fifteenth century. Communities did not vanish with the capital. Noble houses, towns, markets, farms, and regional networks continued in new political arrangements.

Scholars often map post-Mayapán “provinces,” or cuchcabalo'ob, from later testimony. Their borders and internal organization remain debated, and some authority ran through personal relationships rather than tidy territory. A colored reconstruction is a hypothesis about lordship, not a preserved pre-contact road sign.

Towns could include nobles, ritual specialists, farmers, craftspeople, traders, servants, dependents, captives, and visitors, but their political arrangements varied. Archaeology sees buildings and goods more readily than obligations. Later records help, yet Spanish legal categories may distort earlier ranks and relationships.

Columbus sailed in Caribbean waters from 1492 through 1500, but no surviving account records him or another Spanish expedition meeting northern-Yucatán communities then. The famous date belongs in world history without being turned into a local landfall that did not happen.

In July 1502, outside this card, a Spanish expedition encountered a large trading canoe near Guanaja, Honduras. Its cargo demonstrates far-reaching maritime commerce near the period more securely than it identifies every passenger's hometown or ethnicity. Documented Yucatán landfalls followed still later.

sections.title: Step into houselots, kitchens, families, and social differences

items.text: A houselot could combine sleeping space, food preparation, storage, gardens, craft work, shrines, animal care, and gatherings. Archaeological examples from Mayapán mostly predate 1492, so they show a regional inheritance rather than a frozen target-year floor plan. Houses varied in size, materials, and access.

Postholes, plaster floors, hearths, grinding stones, pots, plant remains, bones, tools, and refuse reveal repeated activities. They do not print a family tree. People beneath one roof might be close kin, dependents, visitors, or changing residents, and exact relationships require evidence that ordinary debris rarely preserves.

Later Maya-language wills show women owning, inheriting, giving, and selling property while arranging obligations among relatives. These documents are powerful evidence for colonial Maya lives, not a transcript of 1492 law. They suggest agency and family strategy while also recording a transformed legal world.

Marriage, inheritance, godparenthood, adoption, service, and lineage appear in later records, but conquest and Christian institutions reshaped them. The safest conclusion is that households were social and economic teams whose membership and power differed. A neat modern nuclear-family diagram would hide more than it explains.

House size, imported goods, fine serving vessels, and access to labor can suggest inequality, yet none is a simple wealth meter. One small house might be busy and well connected; one impressive compound could belong to several generations or a noble group. Patterns across many contexts matter.

sections.title: Follow children through learning, chores, stories, and play

items.text: No target-period school roll, timetable, or alphabet exercise survives from northern Yucatán. Children probably learned language, routes, plants, manners, ritual duties, and practical skills by watching, listening, practicing, helping, and being corrected. This participatory model is an inference, not a universal childhood schedule.

Grinding maize, carrying water, tending plants, feeding animals, making cord, fishing, cleaning, trading, and watching ceremonies offered chances to learn in steps. Age, gender, rank, health, and household need probably shaped participation, but later stereotypes cannot assign every child the same chore list.

Elite writing and calendrical knowledge required specialized training, perhaps through households or ritual offices. Surviving books prove sophisticated expertise, but they do not reveal a standard school building, admission age, lesson plan, or the share of children trained. Literacy should not erase other kinds of intelligence.

Miniature vessels, figurines, whistles, and small tools can tempt a toy label. Some may have supported play or teaching; others were offerings, ornaments, instruments, samples, or ritual objects. Context matters, and this card does not hand every small artifact to a child merely because it fits a small hand.

Stories, songs, jokes, local histories, and place knowledge could travel without writing, yet their exact 1490s wording is gone. That absence is not cultural emptiness. It is a preservation limit, reminding us that voices and gestures disappear more easily than limestone walls and broken pots.

sections.title: Plant maize, keep bees, fish, cook, and survive dry seasons

items.text: Maize was central, but evidence and modern comparative research warn against imagining a maize-only diet. Beans, squash, chile, fruits, gathered plants, managed trees, and animals could broaden food supplies. Exact combinations varied by ecology, season, status, trade, crop success, and preservation.

Household gardens, orchards, fields, and productive karst depressions spread risk across different soils and moisture. A rejollada could trap deeper soil and humidity, but not every depression was cultivated identically. Skilled farming meant reading rain, plants, pests, soils, and stored seed rather than following one recipe.

Stingless-bee keeping supplied honey and wax for food, exchange, craft, and ritual. Ceramic hive-related finds and later records make apiculture unusually vivid at Mayapán, though mostly before or after this exact window. Fun fact: a bee can be hardworking without carrying a passport for one “Maya state.”

Coastal and island communities caught fish, collected shellfish, and used marine resources, while inland access differed. Zooarchaeology can identify species and butchery more confidently than a named dish. A fish bone at one port does not establish everybody's dinner across the peninsula.

Grinding maize into dough demanded long, repeated labor; cooking required fuel, water, vessels, timing, and cleanup. Archaeological households reveal tools and debris more clearly than individual cooks or recipes. Ordinary survival rested on dependable staples and countless skilled tasks. The corn never washed its own pot.

sections.title: Find water, protect health, give care, and answer the toilet question

items.text: Northern Yucatán's limestone lets rain drain underground, leaving few permanent surface rivers. Cenotes and wells offered access in some places, while cisterns, reservoirs, jars, and careful collection mattered elsewhere. Water systems were local solutions, not one peninsula-wide utility managed by the atlas polygon.

Chultuns collected rainwater in many dry settings, yet similar underground chambers could store goods or acquire later ritual uses. Shape and context decide function. Calling every cavity a cistern is as risky as calling every modern hole a swimming pool.

Teeth and skeletons can preserve cavities, tooth loss, infection, injury, nutritional stress, and deliberate dental modification. These findings describe sampled individuals at particular sites, often outside 1492 to 1500. They do not diagnose an entire region, and modified teeth were skilled identity work rather than failed dentistry.

Later colonial sources describe herbal knowledge, ritual specialists, childbirth care, and healers, but they were written under conquest, conversion, and translation. They can preserve real Maya knowledge while also reshaping it. No exact-period medical recipe or named practitioner is securely localized to this polygon.

Toilet answer: no reviewed study securely identifies a northern-Yucatán latrine from 1492 to 1500. Much earlier biomarker evidence at San Bartolo in Guatemala suggests pits there received human waste, but importing that toilet across eight centuries and hundreds of kilometers would be historical plumbing malpractice.

sections.title: Work clay, cotton, stone, metal, markets, roads, and canoes

items.text: Potters selected clay and temper, formed vessels, controlled drying and firing, and made wares for cooking, storage, serving, incense, and exchange. Style can reveal communities of practice, but a painted pot does not automatically name its maker's language, ethnicity, gender, or political allegiance.

Spindle whorls and textile tools indicate cotton spinning and weaving, while finished cloth usually decays. Later tribute and trade records show textiles' value, but they cannot assign every loom to women or every garment to one rank in 1492. Tools identify work more securely than workers.

Obsidian and ceramics moved through overlapping regional networks; chemical sourcing and production data help trace some journeys. An imported object demonstrates connection, but it does not prove the owner traveled, spoke the producer's language, or belonged to the producer's political community.

Mayapán preserves specialized effigy-censer manufacture and evidence for metalworking before the target period. These finds show technical knowledge in northern Yucatán, not an uninterrupted workshop schedule in 1495. Craftspeople could relocate, keep working elsewhere, or transmit skills after the capital's political breakup.

Canoes connected coasts, islands, ports, fisheries, and longer trade routes. The large canoe recorded near Guanaja in 1502 carried varied goods and passengers, but it remains later and outside northern Yucatán. It demonstrates maritime capacity near the period, not one route or one political fleet.

sections.title: Read books, count time, visit shrines, and leave an honest writing gap

items.text: Maya scribes used hieroglyphic books to record calendrical, divinatory, ritual, and astronomical knowledge. Surviving manuscripts show sophisticated coordination of signs, numbers, and images across pages. This was a long Maya intellectual tradition, not the work of one unified people inside this polygon.

The Dresden Codex preserves calendrical, divinatory, and astronomical knowledge. Its holding institution gives a broad pre-conquest production range ending around 1521, but no excavated provenance or colophon securely places a page in northern Yucatán during 1492 to 1500. It is nearby-period evidence, not an exact quotation.

The Madrid Codex is usually associated with Late Postclassic Yucatán and records ritual and everyday activities, but its exact production history remains debated. The Maya Codex of Mexico has different dating and provenance problems. “Postclassic” is not permission to print any glyph as 1497.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none securely attributable to northern Yucatán from exactly 1492 to 1500. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. A facsimile of a broadly dated codex can teach about the manuscript tradition, but it cannot become a forged exact-year quotation.

Temples, domestic shrines, caves, cenotes, incense burners, offerings, and calendrical books show that ritual operated at household, town, and regional scales. Meanings changed by setting. Later missionary descriptions can help only when their hostile context and date are made visible.

sections.title: Face conflict, coercion, inequality, and evidence limits

items.text: Mayapán preserves fortification, injuries, desecration, and evidence interpreted as political violence before its mid-fifteenth-century collapse. That history matters to the later regional landscape, but it does not prove every town was fighting in 1492 or that drought mechanically caused one inevitable outcome.

Later colonial records document tribute, alms, cloth payments, and labor demands, but Spanish categories and extraction transformed the system. They do not reveal the precise scale or rules of obligation in each 1490s town. This card names unequal labor without inventing a uniform pre-contact law.

Andrews's revisions to province maps show that regional reconstructions change; later conquest history records negotiation, alliances, and conflict after 1517. Neither source supplies exact 1490s teams or borders. Leaders and communities made choices, but this card does not animate ten years of invented warfare.

Diego de Landa's later, hostile account describes sacrifice under colonial conversion and inquisitorial conditions. It is not a neutral transcript of 1490s Yucatán, and violence cannot serve as a civilization's personality or a funny fact. Exact claims require a named place, date, and evidence trail.

Archaeological wealth, house size, burial treatment, and access to rare goods reveal differences without printing a full class chart. A costly object may reflect office, family, exchange, ritual, or inheritance. Inequality was real, but its meanings and mechanisms have to be argued locally.

sections.title: Celebrate achievements, trace contact, and reject a fake ending

items.text: Achievements included adapting settlement and water use to karst landscapes, connecting communities through exchange, and maintaining sophisticated calendrical knowledge. These depended on farmers, builders, carriers, traders, observers, teachers, and many unnamed workers. No invented empire or single genius is needed to make their collective skill impressive.

The first recorded encounter conventionally linked to Maya traders occurred near Guanaja in 1502. Castaways reached Yucatán in 1511, Hernández de Córdoba's expedition arrived in 1517, and conquest campaigns began later. These dates prevent the atlas's 1500 seam from becoming a false contact ending.

Spanish campaigns in Yucatán were prolonged, violent, negotiated, and repeatedly resisted. Indigenous allies and rivals shaped events, while disease, forced labor, tribute, missionization, and resettlement transformed communities unevenly. This later history must not be compressed into “Spain arrived and the Maya disappeared.”

Maya writers adapted alphabetic writing for wills, petitions, chronicles, town records, and religious texts after conquest. Those documents reveal endurance and creativity while belonging to changed colonial settings. They are invaluable later voices, not substitutes for a securely dated 1490s writing sample.

At 1500 the atlas restores “maya” across many interior probes; it does not document a conquest or collapse. Living Maya communities continue and reshape languages, farming knowledge, arts, scholarship, ceremonies, and family life. The exact id ends in software, while human histories continue beyond every map layer.

ending.text: The atlas removes the exact id in 1500 and assigns many interior probes to “maya.” Nothing in that database boundary records a local fall, migration, or replacement. Towns and households did not vanish because the map changed labels. Living Maya communities and languages also make extinction framing false, although no modern community is an unchanged copy of 1492. This card records an editorial seam rather than a successor state, sudden first contact, or civilization’s end.
